By Dr. Corinna H. Halkios and A. Mark Fendrick, MD

This article was originally published on March 18, 2016 on CardioSource WorldNews.

Two roads diverged into the woods and the United States Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) is taking the road less traveled – and that will, proverbially, “make all the difference.”

In March 2014, President Barack Obama signed the Protecting Access to Medicare Act into law, which included language to create the “Quality Rating System for Exchange Plans” with the goal of developing a system that rates coverage from one to five stars while providing “enrollees in such plans with specific information on such quality ratings.”[3] HHS released a proposed rule for public comment this past year announcing its strategy to develop the star rating system, publishing the final rule earlier this summer.[1] Informed by a study of 154 unique measures used in state-based marketplaces and ratings platforms such as the National Committee for Quality Assurance (NCQA) and the National Quality Forum (NQF), HHS proposed awarding stars based on three core categories and a small number of subcategories. The proposed categories include clinical quality management (e.g. chronic disease management), member experience (patient experience and care access), and efficiency and affordability, which remains unspecified at the moment but may include cost-related plan measurements.[1]

The framework for the system’s design builds on years of prep work – more than a decade’s worth, in fact –particularly informed by a similar system already adopted in the Medicare Advantage market for privately administered Medicare health plans. The Medicare Advantage (MA) star ratings program is a system, initiated in 2008, that rates plans from one to five stars and helps beneficiaries choose and ultimately select high-performing plans. Since the program’s full implementation in 2012, the percentage of enrolled seniors in four-or-more-star (out of five possible stars) plans has increased from 24% to almost 70%,[2] which has saved beneficiaries millions of dollars through higher quality care and lower copayments, while also contributing to a 31% increase in MA enrollment over the past three years.

The final rule HHS released this summer confirms a three-year phase-in period before incorporating efficiency measures into the star ratings, with clinical quality and patient experience measures used to calculate the first display to be implemented in 2017, thus affecting 2016 behavior. Organizations such as the Center for Value-Based Insurance Design Initiative (V-BID Health) have expressed overall general support for the rule, noting that while being preliminary in nature, it does raise crucial issues that require the input of multiple stakeholders. This input is critical at this junction to ensure long-term stakeholder support of the system, to promote plan offerings that improve access and quality while reducing costs, and that forms the basis for iterative updates and improvement.

The long road to value-based care

In addition to introducing quality-of-care metrics into Medicare Part C, the ACA also required HHS to develop a similar system to rate Medicare EBO plans through the Federally Funded Marketplaces. Releasing a preliminary set of measures is crucial to ensuring the quality ratings system is meaningful. The initial, voluntary implementation will establish a stable structure open to stakeholder commentary and HHS reaction, allowing for any necessary improvements before total implementation in 2020.

HHS’ multi-year process is an opportunity to provide feedback on a system that allows consumers to make their own healthcare process changes and emphasizes comprehensive, plan-level assessments. Massachusetts, which has the highest insured population of any state and has served as a general blueprint for the Affordable Care Act as a whole, illustrates that improvement in health coverage markets takes a concerted, community-wide effort. Massachusetts began developing a quality rating system in 2006, before the ACA was implemented at the national level.[3] The systematic, albeit slow, development allowed for stakeholder deliberation and buy-in and for refinements to measures and methodologies so that the new system was more likely to accomplish its goals.

The flexibility allowed via this multi-year phase in will allow HHS to test and improve its measures to award stars, while leaving ample time for states and health plans to engage; this multi-faceted approach is important to gain broad stakeholder support. Incorporating a technical expert panel and explicitly indicating which organizations will be heavily involved, including the NCQA, NQF, the Qualified Health Plan Workgroup (QHPWG), and health insurance issuers, is a good initial step. Over the demonstration period, meeting the core requirements outlined in the CMS Quality Strategy and identifying opportunities for long-term improvement help ensure ongoing intergroup communication and will foster financial sustainability.

Challenges of implementing the program

Although in its early design stages, this quality rating system inevitably will face challenges to achieve its intended purpose: to measure and make available information on the quality of individual qualified health plans at a systematic level.

Standardizing the evidence-based metrics used to assign stars will present methodological challenges. HHS should choose appropriate metrics, ones that provide meaningful information for consumers yet account for the various methods for evaluating care quality and economic outcomes that differ by plan. HHS acknowledges challenges will arise, especially while balancing careful selection of valid metrics with the need for measure parsimony, and has outlined an initial plan with core broad rating measures.

The final rule, released by HHS, reflects concern expressed by many stakeholders during the comment period regarding the availability of adequate data to reliably enable this standardization, and highlights the need for stakeholder engagement and comprehensive data collection as essential tasks during the three-year phase in that will expedite the most important aspect of this plan: the evolution of a fully integrated system that ranks plans based on the value of services provided rather than the volume of services provided.[1]

Why it matters

Unlike the masses of political pledges to repeal the Affordable Care Act, those that propose to introduce value-based insurance design are acts of common-sense, cross-sector stakeholder support. Value-based insurance design (VBID) seeks to change our traditional approach, which focuses on the volume of care, to an approach built around the value of care – that is, the amount of patient-centered clinical benefit achieved for the money spent.3

Our extensive research on value-based insurance design demonstrates that systematically lowering or removing patient financial barriers to those services of the highest value will enhance both quality outcomes and net savings. While VBID programs have been voluntarily implemented and promoted by some private health plans, public and private payers will derive additional benefit through a collaborative implementation process. The quality ratings created in the new HHS system by way of accountable care organizations (ACO) and alternative payment models present one such opportunity to deliver such value to patients and communities, targeting more patient groups with incentives to consume high quality care across all plans, public and private.

Savings generated from treating high-priority conditions with high-value services offer significant potential to reduce overall health care costs. VBID-based cost containment initiatives will not only lead to cost savings, but will also ameliorate the financial toxicity of high out-of-pocket costs, which could bend the trend and make healthcare more affordable for millions.

The Value-Based Insurance Design concept celebrates its tenth anniversary in 2015. Since its inception at the University of Michigan in 2005, V-BID has expanded conceptually and operationally in support of various aims that seek to align patients’out-of-pocket costs with the clinical relative value of specific services. Milestones of V-BID implementation over the past decade are highlighted below.

February 2016: Congress passes the bipartisan “The Trade Facilitation and Trade Enforcement Act of 2015,” (H.R. 644, “Customs Bill”) which includes key V-BID provisions that provide CMS the authority to administer a demonstration to test V-BID in MA. CMS announcement of this landmark five-year demonstration is expected in early 2016, with implementation of MA V-BID plans anticipated in January 2017.

March 2015: HHS comments on V-BID (guidelines on V-BID in Marketplace health plans) concluded in April. This July, the Department released a final rule establishing the method for public information of quality of care of individual and Small Business Health Options Program (SHOP) insurance plans offered through the Exchanges, setting a stage for broad adoption of V-BID outlined in a March letter from the Institute of Medicine Roundtable on Health Literacy. [4,5,6]

Finally, in 2014: Part of the Medicare Advantage V-BID proposal, HHS allows voluntary adoption of state incentive approaches to promote evidence-based care in population health services, including reduced consumer cost sharing for specified services for high-value enrollees.

Full implementation of value-based insurance design will go a long way to solving the paradox of healthcare coverage in America, wherein uncovered people have to make difficult medical decisions based on the price of care. As clinically nuanced design takes greater hold as a solution for a sustainable system and improved consumer choice, it is imperative that payers, providers, and policymakers understand and support these aligned efforts towards value over volume to solve some of our nation’s healthcare challenges. Their efforts will make all the difference.

The panel aims to identify and support costs for “high-value services, treatments, and providers” – and the implementation of value-based insurance design (V-BID) – through incentivizing engagement in clinical healthcare beneficial to patient centered …fulfillment.

V-BID refers to healthcare plans in which “cost-sharing [is] at the consumer level” with value dependent on the value of services being rendered. In these plans, consumers pay little to no additional cost for high-value care recommended by evidence-based guidelines, such as statins for patients with cardiovascular conditions (CVDC) or certain drugs for those with diabetes (see Table 1). By alleviating financial burden, V-BID allows patients to seek the preventive care they need instead of the conflicting consumer behaviors associated with high-cost sharing. Reducing out-of-pocket (OOP) expenses associated with high-quality, high-value care via V-BID improves consumer choice, as well as allows patients the resources to make decisions that lead to healthier outcomes.[3]

Promoting consumer satisfaction and provider collaboration

In 2012, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) announced a value-based purchasing program for Medicare’s hospital inpatient sector, based on performance on quality data metrics.[7,8] This reform incorporated large financial incentives – up to 1.5% of all plan payments proceed to a bonus pool granted to top-tier plans – associated with higher quality ratings, divided into 4 domains: outcomes, patient experience, clinical process, and efficiency. This value-based, program-driven effort demonstrates how systematic implementation of V-BID measures can easily be incorporated to support similar, up-and coming strategies. Early results confirm that private health plans are refining their implementation of V-BID designs with the same systematic support of value-based care across additional patient and disease subsets over time.

Early results from state employee programs can help guide us through broad implementation of benefit design that aligns directly with high-value quality metrics such as improving relevant patient health. There are currently over one dozen states implementing, or in the process of implementing, V-BID programs. Yet the take away from programs like those discussed above remains the need for further integration and personalized incentive processes aligned with ongoing high-value redesign aims to promote stakeholder investments and reduce budget costs.

Emerging evidence demonstrates patients and providers are willing to pay for services with the highest potential for health improvement to prevent more expensive healthcare hazards later on, such as emergency department visits and cancer treatments from CSFs. Financial-related non-compliance serves as a common and compelling motivator for future cost-containing strategies that support patients in making optimal choices for their health.

Coordinating and implementing private and public support of value-based care

Purely economic measures of services’ value to insurance companies and cost-sharing systems that rely on high premiums as a tool to help manage care lead to adverse unintended consequences in patient behavior. Research studies demonstrate that patients respond to higher cost sharing for outpatient care and meds rationally – by lessening their overall utilization not based on need, but according to cost, escalating poor outcomes in cases such as population health programs for high-priority patients (see chart). By incentivizing consumers to consider both costs and associated benefits in value-based care, we’re increasing the effectiveness of healthcare options. First and foremost, the long-term societal savings is too vast to quantify, but we also hope to eliminate the economic barriers that drive many American patients to consume care in ways that are not optimal to their health. The pending state-based quality ratings system currently proposed by HHS could pave a way to health programs that integrate employer and public interest, overall proving the utility of value-based healthcare reform.

Health Affairs Blog, May 22, 2016

The current health care payment and delivery landscape presents a critical opportunity to improve fiscal responsibility and a population’s health. While implementation of benefit designs that encourage people to use high-value medical services has been occurring in commercial and public health insurance markets for decades without needing legislative action, more states recognize the important link between consumer cost-sharing strategies and individuals’ behavior.

Earlier this year, West Virginia lawmakers seized such an opportunity by passing legislation that reduces financial barriers for a set of high-value clinical services that are proven effective in detecting and treating chronic disease. Similar to the Value-Based Insurance Design (VBID) concepts pioneered at the University of Michigan Center for Value-Based Insurance Design, the West Virginia Senate Bill 535 was based on rigorous evidence and broad multi-stakeholder consensus, and will be implemented beginning in 2017.

A retroactive return to the public servant health programs and systems we’re supposed to participate in

Many hold out on seeking care or purchasing prescriptions due to high cost-sharing. In the long-term, avoiding such services increases both economic-customer cost and personal-patient health risk, counterintuitive to the overall goals of our health system. Continued turnover rates reflect the need for real reform in strenuous benefit design, with data showing that over 60 percent of bankruptcies can be attributed to medical costs. Yet administration figures estimate that alternatives like cost-sharing heavily influence the health seeking behaviors of 137 million Americans as individuals have increasingly been required to reach deeply into their own pockets before accessing certain evidence-driven, high-value preventive health services. The same efforts to help offset this cost have reached critical early results in state employee programs (i.e., the Connecticut Health Enhancement Program and the University of Michigan MHealthy: Focus on Diabetes).

West Virginia, though, is now set to lead the nation as the first state that will expand its VBID initiatives beyond state employees to include Medicaid, while also diminishing consumer cost-sharing for certain evidence-based services broadly for individuals enrolled in private, public, and private-public cooperation plans across its state’s extremely diverse health care system.[2] Effective upon implementation by the beginning of 2017, the West Virginia Public Employees Agency will eliminate deductibles, copayments, and coinsurance for alternatives from a list of pre-determined health services considered “high-value” by Medicaid. This change will ensure chronic disease management is affordable, ultimately aimed at reducing high future downstream costs.

The Dialogue Continues

Such patient-centered and cost-conscious approaches highlight the importance associated of logistical coordination. in the push towards value-based insurance care across the full American health system, regardless of plan or network type. On the same day of passage of West Virginia’s landmark bill, Arkansas lawmakers issued the “Arkansas Health and Opportunity for Me Act” (ARHOME), which requires qualified health plans participating in its state partnership to offer at least one VBID benefit through the 1115 waiver demonstration in 2017.[8] While implementing VBID does not require legislative action, states are at varying phases of a broader implementation due in part to policies that historically encouraged utilization of cost-raising and inefficient care services. Arizona, Connecticut, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maine, Missouri, Nebraska, Rhode Island, Tennessee, and Virginia have begun specifically revitalizing their public employee health care programs to reflect similar high-value reform initiatives—but a comprehensive pharmacy benefits program, as in West Virginia, is ripe for evaluation. [3]

The evidence, dedicated work through nine years of legislation in Congress culminating with the federal PPACA, and the uptake at the federal level (e.g. Medicare Advantage) by the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) in National and State demonstration projects alike demonstrates a societal commitment to value-based reform. The achievements of VBID by these state Medicaid and state employee system programs like that of ARHOME and West Virginia likewise highlight the unprecedented opportunity available through further, fully integrated implementation of V-BID across the country’s remaining state markets, ushering in value-based healthcare significant to patient-centered outcomes that matter.

A. Mark Fendrick, MD. Freezing premiums for generic drugs and lowering co-payments for prescription refills are examples of value-based insurance designs that the Congress believes might improve patient outcomes and increase medication adherence for those vulnerable people with select clinical diagnoses. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services has sought comments from the public as it implements H.R. 644 and initiates this voluntary demonstration in 2017, with plans to expand to Medicare Advantage recipients nationwide if successful.[5]

As recently overviewed in the May issue of CardioSource WorldNews,[GR1] we’ve seen recent, substantial innovation in health insurance. Emerging payment models built around the value of clinical services – value-based insurance design or commonly called V-BID – may help alleviate unintended financial barriers that arose with the rapid expansion of cost-sharing strategies. With MACRA reinforcing bipartisan efforts to incorporate V-BID, we highlight five key points on the benefits of the concept.

Honoring the October 2 deadline (90 days after enactment) for MACRA-related comments to specific questions, the Center for Value-Based Insurance Design (V-BID Center) offered responses supported by evidence in the fields of healthcare policy, clinical research, employer-sponsored insurance, Medicare, and Medicaid. First, the team of experts recommended specified alternate, patient-centered payment models target specific services for specific patients, such as those likely to achieve the most clinical benefit from cardiovascular care and medications like statin therapy, as in our pilot study conducted with Aetna. V-BID can address the potential revenue flows to Medicare Balanced options simply by increasing incentives that avoid certain low-value services (e.g. hospitalizations from uncontrolled diabetes) in favor of direct patient coverage for lower cost-sharing, high-value services (e.g. glucose monitoring). These systemic changes improve provider incentives and promote increased focus on preventive disease management over the entire beneficiary population.[5]

Second, a recommendation was made to allow flexibility in design for primary and non-primary services, but limit variations by both services and clinical priority. Constructing highly tailored systems that reduce patient barriers will lead to greater outcomes if health plans can match the evidence- based needs of high priority patients’ access to high-value clinical services. Though the Hawaii 1115 waiver application for patients at risk of Type 2 diabetes, as CMS noted, acknowledges current budget neutrality requirements for such designs, the agency could contribute to long-term benefit and system sustainability if clinically-nuanced V-BID to improve patient choice.[6] Tools such as high-value service frameworks provide practical solutions for testing multiple conditions and services, meeting the flexibility desired but keeping programs manageable; fully implemented and integrated V-BID on a broad basis, such as in Indiana House Bills 1265 and 1269, ensure sufficient funding is redirected to high-value care, which consumers and physicians demonstrate willingness to pursue when barriers are reduced for evidence-based interventions (e.g. statins for CVDC patients).[4, 8]

Third, integrating crucial V-BID programs into current benefit designs would serve to channel individual behaviors towards offering patients the best care for the most affordable price. With regard to VBID, federal oversight and transparency will be needed to determine program enrollees achieve improved outcomes and cost, and differentiate this program from traditional disease management incentives. A holistic list of metrics that includes alternate medical homes for consumers with chronic, high-risk conditions and ongoing CMS plan-level QC alignment efforts could enhance this demonstration’s benefits. Crucially, these would serve as measurement, provider plan, and consumer decision-making frameworks that provide flexibility as to allow ongoing system improvements.

Fourth, the V-BID elements within MACRA and the Medicare Advantage plans can augment the evidence impact of consumer-driven designs and further our understanding of requirements critical to successful results, such as proper evaluation strategies and clear, meaningful measures. CMS should consider incorporating measures beyond Patient Safety and Medication Adherence alone, including Strategy and Alignment Performance methodologies like those devised by the ACP, and those that support more advanced consumer decision-making. [3,7]

Fifth, voluntary implementation of MACRA creates crucial opportunities to engage multi- sectoral stakeholders. By integrating support for patient-centered demands and provider capacity into one joint platform that crosses over payers, stakeholders and the government, we maximize both financial institutional viability and patient health.

Experience from the private sector demonstrates that dually implementing value-based incentives and payment systems can deliver both private and public insurers greater value in care provided and improved patient outcomes. [4,6] V-BID principles mitigate existing cost-related adverse care patterns that leave many without essential services, helping to drive cost savings for providers, payers, and the patient by averting high-cost services downstream (such as hospitalizations) while maximizing individual-friendly choices that lead to optimal overall outcomes.[7] Implementing tried V-BID models that achieve these goals benefit more than insurance programs; a diverse Medicaid landscape, scattered and non-integrated quality measure systems, and recent, continued federal push towards value is clear that comprehensive, systematic change enhances the fiscal, societal, and personal healthcare system for all Americans. [1, 2, 6]

By: Dr. A. Mark Fendrick This post was originally published in Health Affairs Blog, May 12, 2016. Patient empowerment has become a common phrase in health care circles—but what does it actually mean? The phrase is generally framed within two contexts—cost sharing and enhancing the patient “experience.” A recent article in The New York Times compellingly illustrates the shortcomings of our current thinking. The article paints an unfortunate picture of severe financial and personal obstacles, reinforced by our broken paradigm of budgeting and benefit design, exemplified by current high deductible plans.

The Science and Sense of Value-Based Insurance Design

The Value-Based Insurance Design (V-BID) concept, originated at the University of Michigan Center for Value-Based Insurance Design in 2005, argues for transforming health insurance benefits by aligning patients’ out of pocket costs, such as premiums and co-pays, with the clinical value of those services.

 Interventions rooted in V-BID mitigate the adverse medical and financial effects of the existing cost-sharing structure by encouraging patients to use services that generate high levels of clinical value, and discouraging use of services that potentially do harm, provide few benefits, or arise from lack of double communication between patients and providers.

In a recent op-ed for CMWN, we discussed a common, serious example of how cost- sharing that is not aligned with value can harm outcomes and result in waste. Of the hundreds of thousands of Americans who suffer a heart attack every year, very few avail themselves of the high-value medications that lower risk and improve outcomes.[7] This adherence gap prevents optimal outcomes. Proven drugs like beta-blockers, which have been shown effective in reducing the likelihood of further coronary events, require copays that can be too cost prohibitive for even insured consumers to purchase.

An Achievable Solution

Fortunately, employing VBID initiatives in both private and public insurance markets have led to proven success in enhancing clinical care quality and improving value through patient-centered transformation of benefit design for high-value programs. In 2012, CMS announced a value-based payment program that incentivizes hospitals to meet crucial evidence-based measures in quality of care, while many states simultaneously achieved budget savings through V-BID initiatives for their public employee health programs.[8] Over \u02dcfteen states have already begun utilizing VBID interventions in their insured populations to lower patient cost-sharing for high-value services, such as cardiovascular risk assessment programs and diabetes management. Connecticut has recently undertaken this initiative in its employee health plan in its Health Enhancement Program, ensuring lower cost sharing for specified high-value health services including cancer screenings, medications for select diagnoses like hypertension or diabetes, and regular diagnostic procedures such as cholesterol screenings.[7,8]

In an additional demonstration through the University of Michigan’s VBID Center and Aetna, our research team helped coordinate a program to reduce cholesterol medication co-pays and now aim to use those successful findings to replicate such initiatives nationwide as the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid (CMS) implements a similar test by implementing the Volunteer Medicare Advantage pretax V-BID Model.3, 4 Should this nationwide program prove successful to achieve better fiscal and clinical outcomes, over 17 million Medicare recipients could potentially benefit from lower co-pays, reduced cost-sharing, and high-value care integrated into their provider groups through a phased-in plan to coordinate tests, methods, and results between providers and patients.

Enabling coordinated care and resource-conscious spending

The development of infrastructure to broadly implement V-BID integrated with current value-based healthcare models, such as episodes of care similar to the ongoing CMS oncology care model, can decrease the rate of expensive, avoidable hospitalizations and emergency department visits. Savings can then be redirected to preemptive initiatives and other high-value health services that drive tangible population and system benefit like the Kentucky Colon Cancer Screening program currently facilitating integrated colonic early-detection screenings.[8]

The MACRA and Medicare Advantage dual and flexible voluntary strategies allows for this harmonious coordination of stakeholder feedback. This flexibility is a vital signal in establishing a sustainable, viable platform as implementation continues to gain momentum.

Overall, the recent successes of V-BID at state and national levels; the effective, long-term impact of programs such as the MACRA and Massachusetts’ alternative payment models; and West Virginia’s push for V-BID demonstrate an emerging milestone of modern medicine. We are entering historic value-based health care policy design. Continued support from government, insurers, employers, and patients alike will be necessary to provide patient-centered, outcomes-based care across America.

Currently in the World Wide Web, there are a number of blogs that take part with discussions involving the overlooked utility of Siemens Industry Online Support. However, not so many people realize the potential of collaboration between countries in this area.

In May, the Obama administration and the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) provided a plan for the implementation of HR 644. This new provision implements a federally funded 1115 demonstration project beginning in 2017 for select participating states in designated zip codes to test and implement value-based insurance design (VBID) health plans aimed at improving cost and delivery quality. This would apply to Medicare- Advantage enrollees who suffer from high-priority chronic conditions like diabetes and major coronary artery disease (CAD). Results and insights from their observations may provide the basis for evolving the program for broader integration into current health care reform discussions in the United States.

Initial V-BID-related reforms like Connecticut’s Health Enhancement Program demonstrate the potential for transforming budgeting, lowering health insurance premiums, and reducing individual out-of-pocket costs through initiatives at coordinated provider plans.1 Even an intervention as small as lowering the co-pay for high-quality prescribed therapies such as statins could lead to long-term improvement in consumer health conditions, as illustrated from our V-BID Center benefits demonstration with Aetna.[7]The number of state-sponsored VBID programs in place among others implementing first-generation state employee health plan designs has grown to 15, and the flexibility outlined in MACRA’s CMS implementation rule might serve as foundation for even broader public and private V-BID innovation that targets high-value tailored insurance designs, such as Indiana’s recent House Bills 1265 and 1269.2, 4

The United States’ notion of a value-based health care system presents the potential for a radical yet simple evolution towards sustainability as individuals, payers, providers, and the public sector can redefine “value over volume.” Backing for these value-\xadbased reforms by government, and demonstration of added clinician and diverse insurer inclusion, is necessary now more than, ever strive for programs that achieve the best care at the lowest cost.5

This article first appeared in Health Affairs Blog on April 5, 2016 By: Dr. A. Mark Fendrick

Bending the trend of ever-escalating US health care costs is a national priority that involves addressing prices, costs, and quality for patients, providers, and payers toward a value-driven health system. While promising alternative payment models and cost-sharing systems failed to significantly reduce costs or adequately improve Americans’ health and patient satisfaction, a new opportunity has opened to push for broader high-value healthcare curbing greater value through the “quality, not quantity” core model.

In 2013, President Obama signed into law a new provision aimed at encouraging further potential for consumer cost satisfaction without greatly elevating “commonwealth costs. ”Specifically, Section 2713 of the ACA mandated public and private benchmarks for costsharing through its “Quality Rating System for Exchange Plans. ” This program, which –initially includes measures from the National Quality or the American Academy of Family Physicians, began as a voluntary initiative for insurers to designate plan star rankings based on “clinical quality management, ”patient experiences, and “efficiency and affordability,” among others epistemologies.[3]

The exact measures upon which the stars will be rated remain undecided, subject of additional research and interagency input, and HHS will utilize stakeholder input to build a satisfactory, sustainable system prior to a full implementation of the plan in 2021. The availability of such streamlined and evidence-based structures clarifies decision-making for the multi-sectoral consumer, providers, payers and insurers in the delivery of accessible, quality-driven consumer-centric healthcare–the key to the true long-term goals of the ACA itself.

No Greater “Value” Than Consumer Choice

Instituting a system built on clinically-nuanced benefit design would demonstrate the legislature’s commitment to our long-term objective of international competitiveness, improving the poorest American citizens’ health, while achieving the apparent needs for fiscal cost containment related to chronically rising expenditures. While VBID design is often accomplished already in select private insurance markets, states have demonstrated a willingness and ability to implement their own interventions absent legislation through a range of voluntary public-employee strategies (e.g., Massachusetts’s health plan and the Kentucky Colon Cancer Screening Program) with short-term success,[4,5] such as the University’s pilot V-BID program with Aetna that lowered co-pays for statin adherence for its enrollees.[6] The opportunity to quickly eliminate preventive barriers that contributes to higher costs has already proven feasible for states without any legislation necessary, and continues to grow in usage and development. [4] In the absence of legislation, statewide implementation of in-market solutions that address systemic barriers must continue.

The fundamentals seem so obvious. That’s because they are – which means this common sense solution could make the difference to improving benefit and budgetary outcomes. In a new/latest letter to HHS Secretary Sylvia Burwell, delivered on March 11th, the Institute of Medicine’s National Roundtable addressed the misaligned cost-sharing in insurance plans that shifts often risk to the patient, noting the need to “aid [patient] decision-making,” such as medications for high-priority public health patients.[5] Additional efforts align with MACRA’s supports for voluntary innovation on consumer driven payment reforms (CDHP), e.g. coordinated care programs like those high-value population health services for patients suffering from cancer.

Implementing V-BID with single-state plans can address the inefficiencies such initiatives aim to achieve while developing means to align their economic and political interests. Value-based insurance coverage could more accurately reflect the value of spending by substituting low-value for high-value services, returning patient satisfaction to healthcare engagement without driving cost. W. Virginia recently demonstrated bipartisan commitment to this initiative with its passage of Senate Bill 535 this March.[2] Allowing high-value programs to advance consumers’ service satisfaction encourages positive outcomes, such as our findings with diabetes care initiatives in the state of Connecticut.7 The ultimately modest fiscal gains should reflect comprehensive Perspective captures for providers, consumers, and payers that incorporate a lack of resource wastage on inefficient, unnecessary care.

State and federal interest offers a promising path forward into empirically innovative alternatives that illuminate your systems. Medicaid programs, in particular Indiana’s House Bill 1265/1269, suggest the potential exists to develop more integrated planned initiatives together, forming broad frameworks across diverse types together.[8] We need these interventions now, especially when up to 60% of bankruptcies are due to medical bills,[7]to maximize concentrated improvement efforts and consumer engagement. Transitioning towards a value-based landscape that affords patients the most access to care improves our means of achieving sustainable, quality care—and is one investment we can’t afford not to make.

New ACO Proposed Rule Extends the Value-Based Focus of Federal Reform

May 3, 2016

By: Dr. Mark Fendrick


On January 26, 2015, Department of Health and Human Services Secretary Sylvia M. Burwell started our national journey towards value-based health care, announcing an ambitious and defining plan to modify American health care towards high-quality care and strengthening its financial sustainability. Building upon the value-based payment programs authorized in the Affordable Care Act (ACA), her plan called for tying 50 percent of Medicare payments to alternative payment and delivery models by the end of 2018.

This transition is certainly in motion, as reflected when the first Medicare Payment Advisory Commission (MedPAC) public meeting of 2016 focused on designing new alternative payment system frameworks to be implemented as part of the recent Medicare Access and CHIP Reauthorization Act of 2015 (MACRA). That progress continues with the recent release of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services’ (CMS) Next Generation Accountable Care Organization (ACO) final rule. The program builds on the Medicare Shared Savings Program (MSSP) and Pioneer initiatives, and demonstrates government’s growing commitment to designing a value-based health care system that effectively keeps costs down and consumer health and satisfaction up. [1]

As discussed in the CardioSource WorldNews online post “Medicare for More,” the expanded scope of the department’s latest effort, as well as this summer’s newly structured Medicare Physician Fee Schedules (finalized in proposed form on April 27), offer significant opportunity for broadening the federal government’s ongoing health reform framework towards one that encourages a primarily consumer-centric society [textbox: Academic Literature Review of Redesign Reform, March 23]. In Massachusetts, RAND’s research demonstrated significant evidence of early initiatives instituted in its public employee systems designed around high-value plans. After pilot implementation of essential service coverage without out-of-pocket (OOP) costs – or a V-BID system, as we term it– that improved chronic disease eliminated consumer barriers to engagement, outcomes improved, and administrative savings reached over $100 billion.[2]

Motivating Patient Access to High-Value Care

Value-based insurance design, or V-BID, links consumer OOP costs to the clinical valueof a specific test or treatment to improve patient health behaviors and the cost associated with delivering it.[3] By allowing patients to make clinically nuanced wellness choices, key goods can be made both affordable and accessible for the individual’s appropriate health needs without driving costs up, achieving the ACA’s broader objectives of higher quality care, increased experience satisfaction, and fiscal sustainability.

Specifically, the University of Michigan V-BID Center has provided a model to reduce co-pays and deductibles for medications and primary services for those individuals at most risk of high-cost crisis care, while increasing cost-sharing for such services of low value. The potential misalignment in star-rated alternative plan payment for Medicare Advantage (MA) benefits blaze a trail towards a broader era of consumer-driven health policy that may be achieved under a remodel of our payment paradigm with further sustained collaborative innovation.

A breadth of political and profit-driven implementations have already demonstrated the power of our consumer nation to make the choices that incentivize success for patients and benefit budgets. Large insurers like Aetna and states such as Connecticut, Kentucky, and South Carolina put their support and money toward early models of V-BID that incentivize individual OOP payments and physicians to utilize services like diabetic disease prevention and statin adherence3. Massachusetts’ Discount Prescription Drug counter-insurance programs and the state’s health employee V-BID initiative achieved those long\xadterm benefits we seek in supporting personal and public prosperity through healthcare.2

Value-based Health Care’s Time is Now

  Continued breakthrough momentum of models like V-BID is crucial, and with new standards that directly address star-ranking programs to lower baked-in premium costs built as a key deliverable of MACRA, aligning cost-sharing items and quality of care delivery is an easy evolution of current measures instead of existing reimbursement and consumer benefit systems. That’s why flexibility offered in both MACRA’s designs and the ACO rule are promising opportunities to realize VBID’s impact. We have and continue to move towards the future health system that consumers need, but sustained effort and support by clinicians, insurers, patients, policymakers alike is crucial to ensure success. By capitalizing on impactful solutions overdue for implementation, we can creates paradigm revolution in defining the best value from invested expenditures—for taxpayer systems and affordable care, defined ultimately by empowered consumers’ and practitioners’ choices.

The gap of access and need

While medical technology and treatments have advanced nationwide, for many insured individuals with poor prognosis (e.g. diabetes, cardiovascular diseases, cancer), accessing those high-value clinical services that will result in the greatest improvement and wellness is unattainable because of financial cost and misunderstanding of inferior, low quality care that drives consumer behavior. These barriers harm our long-term societal and economic objectives, but patient-centered instead of solely financial benefit insurance initiatives that demonstrate results in both markets illustrate another pathway to achieve quality-driven care.Publically supporting V-BID, such as H.R. 644 and MACRA did through Medicare, shifts the direction of consumer-driven healthcare for its broader American population toward successful, universally-tested alternatives will prove the solution.

To maximize both consumer health and healthcare savings connected, we must streamline communication and accountability from current public and private stakeholders. Patients enabled to seek quality with barriers eliminated, like the Massachusetts employee benefits structure , have the means to participate actively in their own health as partners. States like West Virginia, which passed bipartisan V-BID Senate legislation last month, show the necessity of more cooperative efforts that provide consumers economically meaningful alternatives to fill in coverage gaps inherent in the current care system.[4] Finally, West Virginia’s state effort to address long-term sustainable funding for consumer-friendly benefits program by lowering OOP costs for high-priority service groups, while simultaneously integrating measures within heterogeneous institutions, provides a crucial opportunity to synergize reform initiatives for true long-term goals. [4]

With government and operational, demonstrated support for lower cost-sharing essentials and value-driven innovations, we need to focus upon aligning patients’ out-of-pocket costs with clinical benefit, rather than demanding higher spending and risk in rigid benefit design that fails to deliver consumer satisfaction. By pushing towards this simple change together – as diverse stakeholders – adequately evaluating our systems and preserving active communication during the meaningful benefit design transition that is already ongoing, a better national healthcare alternative is within reach.

Value-based insurance design seeks to change this equation by better aligning consumer cost-sharing with the value of specific health services.[1] Results from three initiatives – state-level reforms to the benefit designs of employee coverage plans, efforts at a national level through the Affordable Care Act (ACA), and the planned implementation of Federation of America (AHIP) each have called for a status quo overhaul of our current system, and MACRA represents the rare legislative opportunity to see that the policy goal of sustainable, high-value coverage centered on our nation’s equally diverse individuals is finally met. [2]

In March, the Center for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) released a proposed rule as part of its innovative approach toward value in pursuit of the three goals established by the administration: increased affordability, improved health outcomes, and higher patient medical experience or satisfaction with care.[3,4] Anchored on a holistic view of patient-centered, evidence-based measures in calculating incentives for Medicare Advantage including cardiovascular disease care, this policy initiative presents a timely opportunity to achieve better quality and alignment for high-impact reform across the remaining inefficient areas of the health care sector.[5]

Individual-Choice, Enabling Infrastructure Design

The current proposed MACRA rule, converting incentives to V-BID style designs for Medicare from its current high cost-sharing strategy, represents a fundamental component of the Obama health care approach: an emphasis on value over increased care, whether that’s in the context of federal, state, or private public-private systems. Converting Medicare cost-sharing structures into a systematic trial that targets sub- groups with low and high levels of cost-sharing for low- and high-value services allows the patient barriers to be removed, maximizing the effectiveness of prevention initiatives, including statin prescriptions (see case study ), or efficiently substitut- ing low-value, high-cost unnecessary procedures for breast cancer diagnosis or treatment.[1] While implementation at this time is purely voluntary, the inclusion of specific population-driven consumer health strategies in the proposed rule indicate CMS still seeks greater innovation in benefit design.

Yet systemic health reform presents complexity, and interdisciplinary cooperation from institutional stakeholders and government agencies will be a critical element in accomplishing MACRA’s success. While our program models within commercial markets achieved some of private employer benefits– structural progress[6] CMS flexibility in measure determination for the three prongs previously mentioned enables similarly positive results. Additionally, including standard guidelines and groups such as HR 644does with its supported 1115 demonstration starting in 2017 and the Institute of Medicine’s National Roundtable healthcare for those at most risk of chronic outpatient diseases.[7,8]

Making Easier Good Choices in Lowering Cost, Elevating Value

Dr. Mark Fendrick, Precision Benefit Design: The Next Frontier in Value-Based Care Video

During the next few years before MACRA’s full implementation, with evaluation of 47 evidential chronic-care outcomes, CMS should also include fiscal and systemic costs as a component of benefit system redesign for consumers to further our understanding of holistic value, encouraging subjective patient engagement measures like feedback and revisiting existing ratings. As demonstrated by our V-BID’s programs in states like Connecticut, Kentucky and South Carolina, creating comprehensive and effective frameworks with targeted benefit and payment designs produces the most savings, labor productivity returns and improved patient adherence as individuals participate in their own health-displaying incentivized demand for evidence-based care, not excessive, low-value alternatives (low out-of-pocket cost sharing for statins or diabetes management, specifically, for high-priority patients with coronary or cardiovascular risk disease have demonstrated staggeringly positive short-term expenses and long-term downstream outcome results). These consumer-directed, enabling initiatives are ones we may implement in our diverse and growing landscape even at a state-level without legislation, as West Virginia demonstrated this March.[6]

A decade of our research demonstrates that coverage completion for individual consumer satisfaction and reduced barriers to evidenced-based care provides institutional-wide value by reducing inefficiencies such as ED visits and opening up funds for effective preventive healthcare. MACRA presents a historical milestone in this movement to achieve affordable choice and quality service for patients through aligned VBID-designed initiatives that can make a real difference for the individual and federal budget priorities through support of systemic restructuring for a truly patient-centered society.

Evidence needed to encourage Medicare Advantage health plans to incorporate high value services within plan design and eliminate wasteful health care spending exists—but political will to enable flexible evaluation is also vital

By Dr. A. Mark Fendrick

Spending on health care rose to over 17% of total US GDP last year, yet tens of millions of the most medically underserved population remains out of reach of critical services that have been proven to positively impact outcomes and economic costs. The federal government recently announced programs to address this imbalance via legislation and new models in the federal regulatory approach to value-based insurance design. Extending the opportunity for public, state employee, private and public-private plans demonstrate the potential for positive systemic transformation if aligned with Affordable Care Act goals.

Signed into law as part of the Trade Facilitation and Trade Enforcement Act of 2015 (H.R. 644, “Customs Bill”), the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services announced in a March 2016 proposed federal regulation that an initial, voluntary Medicare Advantage Value-Based Insurance Design Model (MA-VBID) demonstration program will go into effect in 2017. Building on previous initiatives such as the nine-year Medicare Advantage Quality Rating System or ACA-directed incentives offering private insurance variation, Section 2713 supports innovate benefit design options.[1,2,3]

The proposed value-based initiatives, based on economic and health insurance strategies pioneered by the University of Michigan’s VBID Center starting in 2005, would reduce deductibles and co-payments currently vary state-to-state and plan within a balance of stakeholders and government oversight, charges heavy co\xadpayments even for high quality services. Aligning payments with clinical benefit nursery beds statewide, lowered out-key high-priority service levels strengthens opportunities to avoid crises, prevent hazard or inefficiency of low-value surplus, and improve patient choice of out-of-pocket costs that demonstrable, lead to significant healthfiscalservice demands for maximum satisfaction.4 These value-based designs, implemented across markets, serve to clarify service costs as well quality. Federal backing in H.R. 644 and MACRA outline a prosper- ous path towards future efforts that bridge progress and insured coverage needs in a way that benefits all Americans.

Empowering patients for optimal value

Continued or ignored systemic shifts are increasingly demanding tangible change network-based services in order to maintain three critical insurance deliverables simultaneously: improving quality of care, elevating patient satisfaction with experiences and sustainable revenue costs for both taxpayers and clinical stakeholders.[5] The unfortunate and all-too-common tension between these three elements in concert have failed to adequately deliver real, measurable or effective results, yet ongoing programs based on consumer-coordinated care have and demonstrate the impact set for national reform.

If we’re going to change the pattern of minimal satisfaction paired with poor performance and high costs, augmenting multi-shareholder strategies rooted in MACRA’s voluntary benefit and payment structure while maintaining ongoing program progression and state employee programs is crucial. There is a breadth of political and institutional progress that suggest stakeholder capacity for a fair and patient-center support network already exists, as found with significant cost or resource- based incentives already producing the quality of necessary health consumer care nationwide. In West Virginia, Senate Bill 535, passed with bipartisan support, was the latest effective V-BID initiative that shows additional focused incentive without legislative action leading to positive tangible outcome both in health participation and economic return.[1, 4]

Experience from V-BID Center in diverse programs at the federal and commercial level, such as Kentucky’s Colon Cancer Screening program and the state employees as- sociated with the Michigan-Aetna collaboration, proves that consumers will choose cost-effective solutions and deliver desired results if adequately focused plans allow increased access to achieve value not volume.2 Far-from-stopped progress amid this innovation track indicated in state House Bills like Indiana’s 1265/69[6] illustrate the viable future of the first federal government experiment next year. Only continued public support and sustained feedback through collaborative program refinement will allow these viable models to take us towards sustainable healthcare. These consumer-focused models and regulatory efforts work, and provide us with an imperial means to encourage a prosperous society, one that we can’t afford to lose.

        Enumeration e=node.children();
        
        while(e.hasMoreElements()) {
            
            DefaultMutableTreeNode tmpNode=(DefaultMutableTreeNode) e.nextElement();

        }
